title: How Paul Buchheit became an early YC angel: optimize for learning and push founders to think bigger
summary: Paul Buchheit recounts joining YC's second batch in 2006 by cold emailing, and making early angel bets like Wufoo for a ~50x return. He explains why he optimizes for learning over safety, why startups are a power-law game, and how YC and Standard Capital pump up founder ambition.

principles.text: Cold email the people running something you believe in and offer to help; showing up early opens doors.
principles.quote: I just cold emailed them, introduced myself, and said, "Hey, I'd love to like help out if possible."

principles.text: Optimize for learning: investing some money teaches you things, and playing it overly safe means you never get the experience.
principles.quote: my kind of meta strategy for things is just to kind of optimize for learning. And so, I figure if I just like invest some money, I'll learn something.

principles.text: Startups are a power-law business, so it's fine if most investments are bad as long as a couple are great.
principles.quote: startups are a power law business. So, it's okay if like most of the investments are bad as long as you get a couple of good ones.

principles.text: Be early where consensus sees a joke: most VCs dismissed YC, yet a small early check in Wufoo at ~$1M valuation returned about 50x.
principles.quote: most people in venture thought YC was just some kind of a joke with like horrible adverse selection and no good company will ever apply.

principles.text: Ambition compounds across cohorts: keep raising the bar by showing founders what the best peers are attempting.
principles.quote: part of what we tried to do at YC was always just like pump up people's ambitions. Um and that compounds over batches

principles.text: Make a community of ambitious founders and push them to think bigger; that challenge is much of the value.
principles.quote: we have a community of like really ambitious founders and we bring them together and then we try to kind of like bully them into being more ambitious.
